chapter_sections.label: Definition:
chapter_sections.text:
Geometry is the branch of mathematics that studies shapes, sizes and properties of
figures. The word 'geometry' comes from the Greek words 'geo', meaning the 'earth',
and 'metrein', meaning 'to measure'. EUCLID (325 BCE - 265 BCE), a teacher of
mathematics at Alexandria in Egypt, collected all known work of geometry and arranged
it in his famous treatise called 'Elements' -- thirteen books that influenced the
whole world's understanding of geometry.

chapter_sections.label: Key Points:
points: Geometry originated from the need for measuring land.
It was studied in ancient civilisations: Egypt, Babylonia, China, India, Greece,
the Incas, etc.
Greeks introduced DEDUCTIVE REASONING to establish truth of geometric statements.
Euclid's 'Elements' is divided into 13 books, containing 23 definitions, 7 axioms,
5 postulates, and 465 proved propositions (theorems).
Three undefined terms in Euclid's geometry: POINT, LINE, PLANE.
AXIOMS/POSTULATES are assumed truths (not proved); THEOREMS are proved statements.

chapter_sections.label: THEOREM: (Theorem 5.1)
chapter_sections.statement: Two distinct lines cannot have more than one point in common.
chapter_sections.given: Two distinct lines l and m.
chapter_sections.to_prove: l and m have only one point in common.
proof: Step 1: Suppose, for the time being, that the two lines l and m intersect in two
distinct points, say P and Q.
Step 2: So, we have two lines passing through two distinct points P and Q.
But this assumption clashes with Axiom 5.1 which states that only one
unique line can pass through two distinct points.
(Using Axiom 5.1: Given two distinct points, there is a unique line through them)
Step 3: So, the assumption that two lines can pass through two distinct points is wrong.
We are forced to conclude that two distinct lines cannot have more than one
chapter_sections.hence_proved:
EXAMPLES: (textbook examples -- detailed in Topic 5.2)
EXAMPLE 5.2.1: Proving AB + BC = AC
PROBLEM: If A, B and C are three points on a line, and B lies between A and C
(see Fig. 5.7), then prove that AB + BC = AC.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: From the figure, AC coincides with AB + BC.
(Since B lies between A and C, the total length AC equals AB plus BC)
Step 2: Euclid's Axiom (4) says that things which coincide with one another are
equal to one another.
Step 3: Since AC coincides with AB + BC:
AB + BC = AC
Note: This solution assumes there is a unique line passing through two points.
ANSWER: AB + BC = AC   [Proved using Euclid's Axiom (4)]
EXAMPLE 5.2.2: Constructing an equilateral triangle
PROBLEM: Prove that an equilateral triangle can be constructed on any given line
segment.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: A line segment of any length is given, say AB.
[Fig. 5.8(i): A _______ B]
Step 2: Using Euclid's Postulate 3, draw a circle with point A as the centre and AB
as the radius.
[Fig. 5.8(ii): Circle with centre A, radius AB]
Step 3: Similarly, draw another circle with point B as the centre and BA as the radius.
The two circles meet at a point, say C.
Step 4: Draw the line segments AC and BC to form triangle ABC.
[Fig. 5.8(iii): Triangle ABC formed]
Step 5: Now prove AB = AC = BC (equilateral):
AB = AC, since they are the radii of the same circle (circle with centre A)
...(1)
AB = BC, since they are the radii of the same circle (circle with centre B)
...(2)
Step 6: From (1) and (2), using Euclid's Axiom (1) -- things which are equal to the
same thing are equal to one another:
AB = BC = AC
ANSWER: Triangle ABC is an equilateral triangle.
Note: Euclid assumed (without mentioning) that the two circles drawn with
centres A and B will meet each other at a point.

chapter_sections.label: EXERCISE 5.1.Q1:
chapter_sections.raw:
PROBLEM: Which of the following statements are true and which are false? Give reasons.
(i)   Only one line can pass through a single point.
(ii)  There are an infinite number of lines which pass through two distinct points.
(iii) A terminated line can be produced indefinitely on both the sides.
(iv)  If two circles are equal, then their radii are equal.
(v)   In Fig. 5.9, if AB = PQ and PQ = XY, then AB = XY.
SOLUTION:
(i)   FALSE.
An infinite number of lines can pass through a single point. Through any single
point, lines can be drawn in infinitely many different directions.
(Axiom 5.1 gives uniqueness only when TWO distinct points are given.)

(ii)  FALSE.
Only one (unique) line can pass through two distinct points.
[By Axiom 5.1: Given two distinct points, there is a unique line through them.]

(iii) TRUE.
A terminated line (line segment) can be produced indefinitely on both sides to
form a line.
[By Euclid's Postulate 2: A terminated line can be produced indefinitely.]

(iv)  TRUE.
If two circles are equal, then their radii are equal.
[Two circles are equal when one can be superimposed exactly on the other. By
Axiom (4): things which coincide are equal to one another -- so their radii
must be equal.]

(v)   TRUE.
If AB = PQ and PQ = XY, then AB = XY.
[By Euclid's Axiom (1): Things which are equal to the same thing are equal to
one another.]
ANSWER: (i) False  (ii) False  (iii) True  (iv) True  (v) True

chapter_sections.label: EXERCISE 5.1.Q2:
chapter_sections.raw:
PROBLEM: Give a definition for each of the following terms. Are there other terms that
need to be defined first? What are they, and how might you define them?
(i) parallel lines   (ii) perpendicular lines   (iii) line segment
(iv) radius of a circle   (v) square
SOLUTION:
(i)  PARALLEL LINES: Two lines that lie in the same plane and do not intersect each
other, however far they are extended in both directions.
Terms needed first: line, plane, point, distance.

(ii) PERPENDICULAR LINES: Two lines that meet at a point and the angle between them
is 90 degrees (a right angle).
Terms needed first: line, point, angle, right angle.

(iii) LINE SEGMENT: A part of a line with two endpoints; the shortest path between
two points.
Terms needed first: line, point, endpoint.

(iv) RADIUS OF A CIRCLE: The distance from the centre of the circle to any point on
the circle.
Terms needed first: circle, point, centre, distance.

(v)  SQUARE: A quadrilateral in which all four sides are equal in length and all four
angles are right angles.
Terms needed first: quadrilateral, side, angle, right angle, length.
ANSWER: All five definitions given above. In each case, additional undefined or
previously defined terms are needed.

chapter_sections.label: EXERCISE 5.1.Q3:
chapter_sections.raw:
PROBLEM: Consider two 'postulates' given below:
(i)  Given any two distinct points A and B, there exists a third point C which is
in between A and B.
(ii) There exist at least three points that are not on the same line.
Do these postulates contain any undefined terms? Are these postulates consistent?
Do they follow from Euclid's postulates? Explain.
SOLUTION:
Undefined terms: YES -- 'point' and 'line' are undefined terms (Euclid also kept
these as undefined).

Consistency: These postulates ARE CONSISTENT -- there is no contradiction between
them. Postulate (i) says a third point exists between two given points. Postulate
(ii) says at least three non-collinear points exist. Neither contradicts the other,
and neither contradicts Euclid's postulates.

Do they follow from Euclid's postulates? These postulates do NOT directly follow from
Euclid's five postulates. They are additional assumptions. Postulate (i) deals with
betweenness on a line. Postulate (ii) asserts existence of non-collinear points --
not explicitly in Euclid's five postulates.
ANSWER: Yes, undefined terms exist. The postulates are consistent. They do not directly
follow from Euclid's postulates but are consistent with his system.

chapter_sections.label: EXERCISE 5.1.Q4:
chapter_sections.raw:
PROBLEM: If a point C lies between two points A and B such that AC = BC, then prove
that AC = (1/2) AB. Explain by drawing the figure.
FIGURE: A _________C_________ B   (C is the midpoint, lies between A and B)
SOLUTION:
Given:  A, C, B are on a line; C lies between A and B; AC = BC
To Prove: AC = (1/2) AB

Step 1: Since C lies between A and B:
AC + CB = AB       ...(i)
[AC coincides with a part of AB; by Axiom (4): things which coincide are equal]

Step 2: Given AC = BC       ...(ii)

Step 3: Substituting (ii) in (i):
AC + AC = AB
2 AC = AB
AC = (1/2) AB
[By Axiom (7): Things which are halves of the same things are equal]
ANSWER: AC = (1/2) AB   [Proved]

chapter_sections.label: EXERCISE 5.1.Q5:
chapter_sections.raw:
PROBLEM: In Question 4, point C is called a mid-point of line segment AB. Prove that
every line segment has one and only one mid-point.
SOLUTION:
Given: AB is a line segment.
To Prove: AB has one and only one mid-point.

Step 1: Suppose, if possible, there are TWO mid-points C and D of AB, where C ≠ D.

Step 2: Since C is a mid-point of AB:
AC + CB = AB  and  AC = CB
=> 2 AC = AB    => AC = AB/2       ...(i)

Step 3: Since D is a mid-point of AB:
AD + DB = AB  and  AD = DB
=> 2 AD = AB    => AD = AB/2       ...(ii)

Step 4: From (i) and (ii):   AC = AD

Step 5: But C and D are different points on line AB. If AC = AD, then C and D must
be the same point (only one point on AB can be at distance AB/2 from A).
This contradicts our assumption that C ≠ D.

Step 6: Therefore, our assumption of two mid-points is wrong.
ANSWER: Every line segment has one and only one mid-point.   [Proved]

chapter_sections.label: EXERCISE 5.1.Q6:
chapter_sections.raw:
PROBLEM: In Fig. 5.10, if AC = BD, then prove that AB = CD.
FIGURE: A ____B____C____D   (Four points on a line in the order A, B, C, D)
SOLUTION:
Given:  AC = BD; points in order A, B, C, D on the line.
To Prove: AB = CD

Step 1: Since B lies between A and C:
AC = AB + BC       ...(i)

Step 2: Since C lies between B and D:
BD = BC + CD       ...(ii)

Step 3: Given AC = BD       ...(iii)

Step 4: From (i), (ii), (iii):
AB + BC = BC + CD

Step 5: Subtracting BC from both sides:
AB = CD
[By Euclid's Axiom (3): If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders
are equal]
ANSWER: AB = CD   [Proved]

chapter_sections.label: EXERCISE 5.1.Q7:
chapter_sections.raw:
PROBLEM: Why is Axiom 5, in the list of Euclid's axioms, considered a 'universal
truth'? (Note: the question is NOT about the fifth postulate.)
SOLUTION:
Axiom 5 states: "The whole is greater than the part."

This is considered a universal truth because it holds for ALL kinds of magnitudes --
lengths, areas, volumes, numbers, etc. It is not limited to geometry alone.
Examples:
- If B lies between A and C on a line, then AC > AB (the whole AC is greater than
the part AB).
- If a triangle contains a smaller region inside it, the area of the whole triangle
is greater than the area of the smaller region.

This obvious, self-evident truth applies universally without needing proof. That is
why it is an AXIOM (common notion / universal truth) and not a postulate.
(Postulates are specific to geometry; axioms apply across all of mathematics.)
ANSWER: Axiom 5 ("The whole is greater than the part") is a universal truth because
it applies to all magnitudes -- not just in geometry but in all of mathematics.
That is why it is an axiom, not a postulate.

items.answer:
In Euclid's geometry, three terms are kept undefined: POINT, LINE and PLANE (plane
surface). These cannot be precisely defined without creating an endless chain of
definitions. Euclid represented them intuitively or through physical models. A point
is shown as a dot, a line as a straight mark extending both sides, and a plane as a
flat surface.

Euclid's Postulate 1: A straight line may be drawn from any one point to any other
point.
Axiom 5.1: Given two distinct points, there is a unique line that passes through them.
Note: The postulate says at least one such line exists. Axiom 5.1 (derived from it)
adds that the line is unique -- only one line passes through any two distinct points.

Both axioms and postulates are assumptions accepted without proof. However, POSTULATES
are assumptions specific to geometry (Euclid stated 5 postulates). AXIOMS (common
notions) are universal assumptions used throughout all mathematics, not limited to
geometry (Euclid stated 7 axioms). Today, both terms are used interchangeably.

Axiom (1): Things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one another.
Example: If AB = PQ and PQ = XY, then AB = XY.

Axiom (5): The whole is greater than the part.
Example: If B lies between A and C, then AC > AB (AC is the whole; AB is a part).

---

GIVEN: Two distinct lines l and m.
TO PROVE: l and m have only one point in common.
PROOF:
Step 1: Assume (for contradiction) that lines l and m intersect in two distinct points,
P and Q.
Step 2: This means two distinct lines l and m pass through the same two distinct points
P and Q. But by Axiom 5.1, given two distinct points, there is a UNIQUE line
passing through them. So having two lines through P and Q contradicts Axiom 5.1.
Step 3: Therefore, the assumption is wrong. We conclude that two distinct lines cannot
have more than one point in common.
HENCE PROVED.

GIVEN: Points A, B, C on a line; B lies between A and C.
TO PROVE: AB + BC = AC.
PROOF:
Step 1: From the figure, the segment AC coincides with AB + BC, since B divides AC
into two parts AB and BC.
Step 2: By Euclid's Axiom (4): "Things which coincide with one another are equal to
one another."
Step 3: Since AC coincides with AB + BC:
AB + BC = AC
Note: This proof assumes a unique line passes through any two points.
HENCE PROVED.

---

GIVEN: A line segment AB of any length.
TO PROVE: An equilateral triangle ABC can be constructed on AB.
CONSTRUCTION:
Step 1: Using Euclid's Postulate 3, draw a circle with centre A and radius AB.
Step 2: Using Euclid's Postulate 3, draw another circle with centre B and radius BA.
Step 3: Let the two circles meet at point C.
Draw line segments AC and BC. Triangle ABC is formed.
PROOF:
Step 4: AB = AC (both are radii of the circle with centre A)         ...(1)
Step 5: AB = BC (both are radii of the circle with centre B)         ...(2)
Step 6: From (1) and (2), applying Euclid's Axiom (1) -- things which are equal to
the same thing are equal to one another:
AB = BC = AC
Step 7: Since all three sides are equal, triangle ABC is equilateral.
HENCE PROVED.
Note: Euclid assumed (without mentioning) that the two circles drawn with centres
A and B will meet each other at a point.

GIVEN: Four points A, B, C, D on a line in the order A, B, C, D; and AC = BD.
TO PROVE: AB = CD.
FIGURE: A ____B____C____D
PROOF:
Step 1: Since B lies between A and C on the line:
AC = AB + BC       ...(i)
[B divides AC into AB and BC]
Step 2: Since C lies between B and D on the line:
BD = BC + CD       ...(ii)
[C divides BD into BC and CD]
Step 3: It is given that:
AC = BD            ...(iii)
Step 4: Substituting (i) and (ii) in (iii):
AB + BC = BC + CD
Step 5: By Euclid's Axiom (3) -- "If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders
are equal" -- subtracting BC from both sides:
AB = CD
HENCE PROVED.

PART 1 -- Proving AC = (1/2) AB:
GIVEN: Points A, C, B on a line; C lies between A and B; AC = BC.
TO PROVE: AC = (1/2) AB.
FIGURE: A ______C______ B

Step 1: Since C lies between A and C:
AC + CB = AB       ...(i)
[By Axiom (4): AC coincides with part of AB, so AC + CB = AB]
Step 2: Given AC = BC              ...(ii)
Step 3: Substituting (ii) in (i):
AC + AC = AB
2 AC = AB
AC = (1/2) AB
[By Axiom (7): Things which are halves of the same things are equal]
HENCE PROVED.

PART 2 -- Every line segment has only one mid-point:
Step 4: Suppose, if possible, AB has TWO mid-points C and D (C ≠ D).
Step 5: Since C is mid-point: 2 AC = AB  =>  AC = AB/2      ...(iii)
Since D is mid-point: 2 AD = AB  =>  AD = AB/2      ...(iv)
Step 6: From (iii) and (iv): AC = AD.
But C and D are distinct points on AB -- only one point on AB can be at
distance AB/2 from A. This is a contradiction.
Step 7: Therefore the assumption is wrong. Every line segment has one and only one
mid-point.
HENCE PROVED.

---

PART A — Development of Geometry Across Civilisations:

Geometry originated from the need for measuring land. The word 'geometry' comes from
Greek words 'geo' (earth) and 'metrein' (to measure). It was studied in various ancient
civilisations:

1. Egyptian Civilisation:
The Egyptians developed geometry mainly because of flooding by the river Nile, which
wiped out field boundaries. They developed techniques for calculating areas and for
constructing canals and pyramids. They also knew the formula for the volume of a
truncated pyramid.

2. Indus Valley Civilisation (about 3000 BCE):
Excavations at Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro show extensive use of geometry. Cities were
well planned with parallel roads and drainage systems. Bricks had a fixed ratio of
length : breadth : thickness = 4 : 2 : 1.

3. Ancient India -- Sulbasutras (800 BCE to 500 BCE):
The Sulbasutras were manuals of geometrical constructions for building altars (vedis).
The Sriyantra from the Atharvaveda consists of nine interwoven isosceles triangles
producing 43 subsidiary triangles. Accurate geometric methods were used but the
reasoning behind them was not discussed.

4. Babylonians and Egyptians:
Both civilisations used geometry mostly for practical purposes -- calculating areas,
volumes, and for constructions. There were no general rules or proofs.

5. Greek Civilisation -- Key Difference:
The Greeks were the first to emphasise the REASONING behind geometric constructions.
They were interested in establishing the TRUTH of geometric statements using
deductive reasoning. Thales (640-546 BCE) gave the first known proof -- that a
circle is bisected by its diameter. Pythagoras (572 BCE), his famous pupil,
discovered many geometric properties.

Euclid (325-265 BCE), teacher at Alexandria, collected all known geometry into
'Elements' -- 13 books -- which influenced the world's understanding of geometry.

PART B — Euclid's Approach: Definitions, Axioms, Postulates and Theorems:

1. Definitions:
Euclid gave 23 definitions in Book 1 of 'Elements'. Some important ones:
- A point is that which has no part.
- A line is breadthless length.
- A straight line lies evenly with the points on itself.
- A surface has length and breadth only.

2. Undefined Terms:
Some terms like 'point', 'line' and 'plane' cannot be defined precisely without
creating a never-ending chain of definitions. So they are kept as UNDEFINED TERMS.
We represent them intuitively using physical models (a dot for point, a straight
mark for line, a flat surface for plane).

3. Euclid's 7 Axioms (Common Notions -- true throughout all mathematics):
(1) Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another.
(2) If equals are added to equals, wholes are equal.
(3) If equals are subtracted from equals, remainders are equal.
(4) Things which coincide are equal to one another. [Justifies superposition]
(5) The whole is greater than the part.
(6) Things double of the same things are equal.
(7) Things half of the same things are equal.

4. Euclid's 5 Postulates (specific to geometry):
Postulate 1: A straight line may be drawn from any point to any other point.
Postulate 2: A terminated line can be produced indefinitely.
Postulate 3: A circle can be drawn with any centre and any radius.
Postulate 4: All right angles are equal to one another.
Postulate 5: (Parallel postulate -- most complex) If a straight line falling on two
straight lines makes interior angles on the same side less than two right angles,
the two lines meet on that side if produced indefinitely.

5. Theorems (Propositions):
Starting from axioms, postulates, and definitions, Euclid PROVED 465 propositions
(theorems) using deductive reasoning. Theorems are not assumed -- they are derived
through logical steps. Example: Theorem 5.1 proves that two distinct lines cannot
have more than one point in common (proved using Axiom 5.1).

6. Consistent System:
A system of axioms is consistent if no contradiction can be deduced from them.
Euclid's system is consistent.

items.question: The word 'geometry' comes from Greek words meaning:
items.explanation: Geo = 'earth', metrein = 'to measure' in Greek. Geometry literally means 'earth measurement'.

items.question: Euclid's 'Elements' was divided into how many books?
items.explanation: Euclid's 'Elements' was organised into 13 books, covering plane geometry, number theory, and solid geometry.

items.question: Point, line and plane in Euclid's geometry are taken as:
items.explanation: Point, line and plane cannot be precisely defined using simpler terms; they are taken as undefined (primitive) terms in Euclid's geometry.

items.question: How many postulates did Euclid state?
items.explanation: Euclid stated exactly 5 postulates, which are assumptions specific to geometry.

items.question: How many axioms (common notions) did Euclid state?
items.explanation: Euclid stated 7 axioms (common notions), which are general truths applicable to all of mathematics.

items.question: Which postulate of Euclid is used in constructing an equilateral triangle on a given line segment?
items.explanation: Postulate 3 allows drawing a circle with any centre and any radius — used to draw arcs in the equilateral triangle construction.

items.question: Euclid's 'Elements' consists of how many books?
items.explanation: Euclid's 'Elements' has 13 books — same as CHAPTER:2 above (consistent answer).

items.question: In Example 5.2.1, AB + BC = AC is proved using Euclid's:
items.explanation: Axiom (4) states: 'Things which coincide with one another are equal to one another.' AC = AB + BC when B is between A and C.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT one of Euclid's five postulates?

options.A: A straight line may be drawn from any one point to any other point.
options.B: All right angles are equal to one another.
options.C: Things which coincide with one another are equal to one another.
options.D: A terminated line can be produced indefinitely.

items.explanation: This is Axiom 4, NOT a postulate

items.question: Axiom 5.1 states that given two distinct points, the line through them is:
items.explanation: Axiom 5.1: Given two distinct points, there is one and only one (unique) line passing through them.

items.question: Theorem 5.1 (two distinct lines cannot have more than one point in common) is proved using:

options.A: Axiom (1) -- things equal to the same thing are equal
options.B: Postulate 4 -- all right angles are equal
options.C: Axiom 5.1 -- given two distinct points, there is a unique line through them
options.D: Axiom (5) -- the whole is greater than the part

items.explanation: Theorem 5.1 is proved using Axiom 5.1 — if two lines intersected at two points, both points would lie on two distinct lines, contradicting Axiom 5.1.

items.question: How many definitions did Euclid state in Book 1 of the 'Elements'?
items.explanation: Euclid stated 23 definitions in Book 1, starting with the definition of a point as 'that which has no part'.

sections.label: Definition:
sections.text:
Geometry appears to have originated from the need for measuring land. The word
'geometry' comes from the Greek words 'geo', meaning the 'earth', and 'metrein',
meaning 'to measure'. This branch of mathematics was studied in various forms in
every ancient civilisation, be it in Egypt, Babylonia, China, India, Greece, the
Incas, etc. The people of these civilisations faced several practical problems which
required the development of geometry in various ways.

sections.label: Key Points:
points: EGYPTIAN CIVILISATION: Used geometry to redraw field boundaries after Nile flooding;
also used for computing volumes of granaries, constructing canals and pyramids.
Knew formula for volume of truncated pyramid (Fig. 5.1).
INDUS VALLEY CIVILISATION (about 3000 BCE): Extensive use of geometry. Cities well
planned, roads parallel, underground drainage. Brick ratio length:breadth:thickness
= 4:2:1. Skilled in mensuration and practical arithmetic.
SULBASUTRAS (800 BCE - 500 BCE): Indian manuals of geometrical constructions for
building vedis (altars). Sriyantra from Atharvaveda = 9 interwoven isosceles
triangles producing 43 subsidiary triangles.
ANCIENT WORLD: Geometry passed unsystematically -- orally or through palm leaf
messages. Babylonians and Egyptians used geometry only for practical purposes.
GREECE: Greeks emphasised REASONING behind constructions. Interested in deductive
reasoning to establish truth.
THALES (640 BCE - 546 BCE): First known proof -- that a circle is bisected by its
diameter. Pythagoras (572 BCE) was his famous pupil.
EUCLID (325 BCE - 265 BCE): Teacher at Alexandria, Egypt. Collected all known
geometry into 'Elements' (13 books). Influenced world's understanding of geometry.

items.answer:
The word 'geometry' comes from the Greek words 'geo', meaning the 'earth', and
'metrein', meaning 'to measure'. Geometry appears to have originated from the need
for measuring land. It was studied in various forms across ancient civilisations
including Egypt, Babylonia, India, Greece and the Incas.

The bricks used for constructions in the Indus Valley Civilisation were kiln fired.
The ratio of length : breadth : thickness of the bricks was found to be 4 : 2 : 1.
This shows that the town dwellers of this civilisation (about 3000 BCE) were skilled
in mensuration and practical arithmetic, and cities like Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro
were highly organised and well planned.

Thales (640 BCE - 546 BCE) was a Greek mathematician. He is credited with giving the
first known proof in mathematics. His proof was that a circle is bisected (cut into
two equal parts) by its diameter. One of his most famous pupils was Pythagoras
(572 BCE), who along with his group discovered many geometric properties.

The sriyantra (given in the Atharvaveda) consists of nine interwoven isosceles
triangles arranged in such a way that they produce 43 subsidiary triangles. It was
used as a pattern for altars required for public worship. These altars whose shapes
were combinations of rectangles, triangles and trapeziums required accurate geometric
methods for construction.

---

GIVEN: Information about Sulbasutras and Vedic geometry from the textbook.
DESCRIPTION:
Step 1: The Sulbasutras (800 BCE to 500 BCE) were the manuals of geometrical
constructions in ancient India. The word means 'rules of the cord' (cord was
used for measurement).
Step 2: The geometry of the Vedic period originated with the construction of altars
(or vedis) and fireplaces for performing Vedic rites. The location of the
sacred fires had to be in accordance with clearly laid down instructions about
their shapes and areas.
Step 3: Square and circular altars were used for household rituals. Altars whose shapes
were combinations of rectangles, triangles and trapeziums were required for
public worship. Accurate geometric methods were used for construction of these
altars. However, the principles (reasoning) behind them were not discussed.

COMPARISON:
Step 1: Babylonians and Egyptians used geometry mostly for practical purposes -- such
as calculating areas, volumes, and constructing buildings. The geometry developed
by Egyptians mainly consisted of statements of results with no general rules or
reasoning behind them.
Step 2: In civilisations like Greece, the emphasis was on the REASONING behind why
certain constructions work. The Greeks were interested in establishing the TRUTH
of statements they discovered using deductive reasoning. This made geometry a
systematic science.
Step 3: Euclid (325-265 BCE), teacher at Alexandria in Egypt, collected all known work
of geometry and arranged it in his famous treatise called 'Elements' -- 13 books.
He used axioms, postulates, and definitions to logically prove 465 propositions
(theorems). These books influenced the whole world's understanding of geometry
for generations to come.

---

PART 1 — Indus Valley Civilisation (about 3000 BCE):
Step 1: Excavations at Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro show that the Indus Valley Civilisation
made extensive use of geometry. It was a highly organised society.
Step 2: The cities were highly developed and very well planned. The roads were parallel
to each other and there was an underground drainage system. The houses had many
rooms of different types.
Step 3: Town dwellers were skilled in mensuration and practical arithmetic. The bricks
used for constructions were kiln fired and the ratio length : breadth : thickness
was 4 : 2 : 1 -- showing standardised manufacturing.
Step 4: These features show that geometry was being used practically and systematically,
though without formal proofs.

PART 2 — Ancient India: Sulbasutras (800 BCE to 500 BCE):
Step 5: The Sulbasutras were the manuals of geometrical constructions. The geometry of
the Vedic period originated with the construction of altars (vedis) and
fireplaces for performing Vedic rites.
Step 6: Square and circular altars were used for household rituals. Altars combining
rectangles, triangles and trapeziums were required for public worship. The
Sriyantra from the Atharvaveda had nine interwoven isosceles triangles producing
43 subsidiary triangles.
Step 7: Accurate geometric methods were used for altar construction. However, the
principles behind them were not discussed -- the 'why' was not explored.
Step 8: Conclusion: Both civilisations used geometry for highly practical and organised
purposes. Though the methods were accurate, geometry was not yet developed into
a systematic science with formal proofs.

Step 1: EGYPT -- Practical Origins:
Geometry began as a practical tool in Egypt. The river Nile overflowed each
year, wiping out field boundaries. Egyptians developed geometric techniques to
redraw these boundaries and to calculate areas. They also used geometry for
computing volumes of granaries, constructing canals and pyramids. They even knew
the formula for the volume of a truncated pyramid.

Step 2: ANCIENT INDIA (Sulbasutras, 800-500 BCE):
In India, the Sulbasutras were manuals of geometrical constructions. Geometry
was used to build altars of specific shapes for Vedic rites. Accurate methods
were used but the underlying principles were not explained.

Step 3: BABYLONIA AND INDIA/ROME:
In civilisations like Babylonia, geometry remained a practical discipline. The
geometry developed by Egyptians mainly consisted of statements of results.
There were no general rules of procedure. Babylonians and Egyptians used
geometry for practical purposes and did little to develop it as a systematic
science.

Step 4: GREECE -- Reasoning and Deductive Proof:
In Greece, the emphasis shifted to the REASONING behind geometric constructions.
The Greeks were interested in establishing the truth of geometric statements
using deductive reasoning. Thales (640-546 BCE) gave the first known proof --
that a circle is bisected by its diameter. Pythagoras (572 BCE) and his group
discovered many geometric properties.

Step 5: EUCLID (325-265 BCE) -- The Systematic Foundation:
Euclid, teacher at Alexandria in Egypt, collected all known work of geometry
and arranged it in his famous treatise 'Elements' -- 13 books. He stated 23
definitions, 7 axioms (common notions), 5 postulates, and proved 465
propositions (theorems) by deductive reasoning.
Significance: Euclid's systematic approach -- starting from a few assumed truths
(axioms and postulates) and logically proving everything else -- became the
model for all of mathematics. His 'Elements' influenced the world's understanding
of geometry for over 2000 years.

Step 1: DEDUCTIVE REASONING -- Definition:
Deductive reasoning is the process of reaching a certain conclusion from a set
of accepted facts (axioms, postulates) using logical steps. Each step in the
argument follows necessarily from the previous steps. The conclusion is
guaranteed to be true if the starting facts are true.

Step 2: EGYPTIANS AND BABYLONIANS:
These civilisations used geometry entirely for practical purposes. Their geometry
consisted mainly of statements of results -- "do this to get that" -- without
any explanation of WHY it works. There were no general rules of procedure. They
did not use deductive reasoning to prove their results.

Step 3: GREEKS:
In contrast, the Greeks were interested in establishing the TRUTH of geometric
statements. They used deductive reasoning -- starting from accepted truths and
logically deriving new results. This made geometry a rigorous, systematic science.
Thales gave the first known proof (circle bisected by diameter). Euclid built
an entire system of geometry on this foundation.

Step 4: EXAMPLE -- Deductive Reasoning in Euclid:
Proving AB + BC = AC (Example 5.2.1):
- Accepted fact (Axiom 4): Things that coincide are equal to one another.
- Observation: In the figure, AC coincides with AB + BC (since B lies between
A and C).
- Deductive conclusion: Therefore AB + BC = AC.
This is a simple example of how a fact (axiom) is used to derive a new result
(conclusion) through logical reasoning -- the essence of deductive reasoning.

---

PART A — Development of Geometry from Egypt to Greece:

Geometry developed across civilisations out of practical necessity. The word 'geometry'
comes from Greek 'geo' (earth) and 'metrein' (to measure) -- it literally began as
the science of measuring land.

1. EGYPT:
The Egyptians developed geometry because the river Nile flooded every year and wiped
out the boundaries between adjoining fields. After each flooding, boundaries had to
be redrawn. For this purpose, Egyptians developed techniques for calculating areas
and doing simple constructions. They also used geometry for computing volumes of
granaries and constructing canals and pyramids. They knew the correct formula to find
the volume of a truncated pyramid (Fig. 5.1). However, Egyptian geometry mainly
consisted of statements of results -- there were no general rules of procedure.

2. BABYLONIA:
Babylonians also used geometry mostly for practical purposes. Like Egyptians, they
did not develop a system with general rules or proofs. Geometry remained a practical,
unsystematic discipline.

3. ANCIENT INDIA:
The Sulbasutras (800-500 BCE) were manuals of geometrical constructions for building
altars (vedis) for Vedic rites. The Sriyantra from Atharvaveda had nine interwoven
isosceles triangles producing 43 subsidiary triangles. Accurate methods were used but
the reasoning behind them was not discussed. The Indus Valley Civilisation (3000 BCE)
used geometry for city planning, standardised bricks (ratio 4:2:1), and drainage.

4. GREECE -- KEY SHIFT:
The crucial difference in Greece was the emphasis on REASONING. While Babylonians
and Egyptians focused on what works, the Greeks focused on WHY it works. The Greeks
were interested in establishing the TRUTH of statements using DEDUCTIVE REASONING.
Geometry shifted from a practical tool to a rigorous logical science. This is the
most important development in the history of geometry.

PART B — Thales, Pythagoras and Euclid:

1. THALES (640 BCE - 546 BCE):
Thales was a Greek mathematician who is credited with giving the FIRST KNOWN PROOF
in mathematics. He proved that a circle is bisected (cut into two equal halves) by
its diameter. This was revolutionary -- instead of just observing a result, he
proved it using reasoning. Thales showed that geometric truths can be established
through logical argument.

2. PYTHAGORAS (572 BCE):
Pythagoras was one of Thales' most famous pupils. He and his group (the Pythagoreans)
discovered many geometric properties and developed the theory of geometry to a great
extent. Their work continued till about 300 BCE and formed a major part of the
geometric knowledge that Euclid later compiled.

3. EUCLID (325 BCE - 265 BCE) and 'ELEMENTS':
At the time of 300 BCE, Euclid, a teacher of mathematics at Alexandria in Egypt,
collected all the known work of geometry and arranged it in his famous treatise
called 'Elements'. He divided 'Elements' into thirteen chapters, each called a book.

What made 'Elements' extraordinary:
- He started with just 23 definitions, 7 axioms (common notions), and 5 postulates.
- From these few starting points, he logically proved 465 propositions (theorems).
- Every theorem was proved using only the axioms, postulates, definitions, and
previously proved theorems -- nothing was assumed without justification.
- This systematic, deductive approach became the model for all of mathematics.

SIGNIFICANCE:
Euclid's 'Elements' is one of the most influential works in the history of
mathematics. It influenced the whole world's understanding of geometry for
generations. Even today, the geometry we study in school is essentially Euclid's
geometry. His method of logical proof from a few axioms became the foundation of
modern mathematics and science.

sections.label: Definition:
sections.text:
AXIOMS or POSTULATES are the assumptions which are obvious universal truths. They are
not proved. THEOREMS (also called PROPOSITIONS) are statements which are proved using
definitions, axioms, previously proved statements and deductive reasoning. Euclid used
this system to build geometry from first principles -- starting with 23 definitions,
7 axioms, and 5 postulates, he deduced 465 propositions.

sections.label: Key Points:
points: Euclid's approach: geometry as an abstract model of the world.
solids (3D) -> surfaces (2D) -> lines (1D) -> points (0D) [lose one dimension each step]
Euclid gave 23 DEFINITIONS; 7 are given below.
Some terms (point, line, plane) kept as UNDEFINED TERMS -- defining them leads to an
infinite chain of definitions.
7 AXIOMS (common notions) apply throughout mathematics (not geometry-specific).
5 POSTULATES are specific to geometry.
Postulate 5 is far more complex than Postulates 1-4.
AXIOM 5.1: Given two distinct points, there is a unique line through them.
CONSISTENT system: impossible to deduce a contradiction from the axioms.

sections.label: LIST OF SUB TOPICS IN THIS TOPIC:
items: (Mode B: No sub-topics in textbook for Topic 5.2 -- none added)

sections.label: FORMULA: (Not applicable -- this topic covers definitions, axioms, postulates, theorems)
THEOREM: (Theorem 5.1)
sections.statement: Two distinct lines cannot have more than one point in common.
sections.given: Two distinct lines l and m.
sections.to_prove: l and m have only one point in common.
proof: Step 1: Assume (for contradiction) that lines l and m intersect in two distinct points
(Assumption: two lines pass through the same two distinct points P and Q)
Step 2: But Axiom 5.1 states that given two distinct points, there is a UNIQUE line
(This means only one line can pass through both P and Q)
Step 3: Having two lines through the same two points contradicts Axiom 5.1.
Therefore the assumption in Step 1 is wrong.
Step 4: We conclude that two distinct lines cannot have more than one point in common.
sections.hence_proved:
EXAMPLES:
EXAMPLE 5.2.1: Proving AB + BC = AC
PROBLEM: If A, B and C are three points on a line, and B lies between A and C
(see Fig. 5.7), then prove that AB + BC = AC.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: In the figure, AC coincides with AB + BC.
(B lies between A and C; point A to C spans AB then BC)
Step 2: By Euclid's Axiom (4): things which coincide with one another are equal to
one another.
Step 3: Since AC coincides with AB + BC:
AB + BC = AC
ANSWER: AB + BC = AC   [Proved using Euclid's Axiom (4)]
EXAMPLE 5.2.2: Constructing an equilateral triangle on a given line segment
PROBLEM: Prove that an equilateral triangle can be constructed on any given line
segment.
SOLUTION:
Step 1: Given: A line segment AB.  [Fig. 5.8(i): A _______ B]
Step 2: Using Euclid's Postulate 3, draw a circle with centre A and radius AB.
[Fig. 5.8(ii)]
Step 3: Using Euclid's Postulate 3 again, draw a circle with centre B and radius BA.
The two circles intersect at a point, say C.
Step 4: Draw line segments AC and BC to form triangle ABC.  [Fig. 5.8(iii)]
Step 5: Prove equilateral (AB = AC = BC):
AB = AC  (both are radii of the circle with centre A)    ...(1)
AB = BC  (both are radii of the circle with centre B)    ...(2)
Step 6: By Axiom (1) -- things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one
another: from (1) and (2), AB = BC = AC.
ANSWER: Triangle ABC is equilateral.
[Note: Euclid assumed the two circles meet at a point, without proving it.]
ADDITIONAL CALCULATIONS:
Problem 1: [Application of Euclid's Axiom (3)]
If 2x + 3 = 11, find the value of x using Euclid's Axioms.
Solution:
Step 1: Given: 2x + 3 = 11
Step 2: By Axiom (3) -- if equals are subtracted from equals, remainders are equal.
Subtract 3 from both sides:
2x + 3 - 3 = 11 - 3
2x = 8
Step 3: By Axiom (7) -- things which are halves of the same things are equal.
Take half of both sides:
x = 4
Answer: x = 4
Problem 2: [Application of Axiom 5.1]
How many lines can pass through two distinct points A and B? How many lines can pass
through a single point P?
Solution:
Step 1: By Axiom 5.1: Given two distinct points, there is a UNIQUE line through them.
So, through points A and B, exactly ONE line can pass.
Step 2: Through a single point P, infinitely many lines can pass (in all directions).
(Axiom 5.1 gives uniqueness only when two distinct points are given.)
Answer: Through two distinct points: exactly 1 line.
Through a single point: infinitely many lines.

items.answer:
Undefined terms are geometric terms kept without definition because defining them leads
to a never-ending chain of definitions. In Euclid's geometry, three terms are kept
undefined: POINT, LINE and PLANE (plane surface). We can only represent them intuitively
-- a point as a dot, a line as a straight endless mark, and a plane as a flat surface.

Euclid's POSTULATES (5 in number) are assumptions specific to geometry -- for example,
"a straight line may be drawn from any one point to any other point."
AXIOMS (7 in number, called common notions) are assumptions used throughout all of
mathematics, not limited to geometry -- for example, "the whole is greater than the
part." Today, both terms are used interchangeably.

Euclid's Postulate 1: A straight line may be drawn from any one point to any other
point. (This guarantees at least one line exists through two distinct points.)
Axiom 5.1: Given two distinct points, there is a unique line that passes through them.
(This adds uniqueness -- only one line through two distinct points.)
Euclid frequently assumed this uniqueness (Axiom 5.1) without stating it explicitly.

A system of axioms is called CONSISTENT if it is impossible to deduce from these axioms
a statement that contradicts any axiom or previously proved statement. In other words,
no contradiction can arise from the system. When any system of axioms is given, it must
be verified that the system is consistent. Euclid's system of axioms is consistent.

---

GIVEN: Two distinct lines l and m.
TO PROVE: l and m have only one point in common.
PROOF:
Step 1: Suppose (for contradiction) that the two lines l and m intersect in two distinct
points, say P and Q.
Step 2: This means two distinct lines pass through the same two distinct points P and Q.
But by Axiom 5.1 -- "Given two distinct points, there is a UNIQUE line through
them" -- only one line can pass through P and Q. Having two such lines
contradicts Axiom 5.1.
Step 3: Therefore, the assumption is wrong. Two distinct lines cannot have more than
one point in common.
HENCE PROVED.

GIVEN: AB is a line segment.
TO PROVE: AB has one and only one mid-point.
PROOF:
Step 1: Suppose (for contradiction) that AB has TWO mid-points C and D, where C ≠ D.
Step 2: Since C is a mid-point:
AC + CB = AB  and  AC = CB
=> 2 AC = AB  =>  AC = AB/2       ...(i)
Since D is a mid-point:
AD + DB = AB  and  AD = DB
=> 2 AD = AB  =>  AD = AB/2       ...(ii)
Step 3: From (i) and (ii): AC = AD.
But C and D are distinct points on AB. Only one point can be at distance AB/2
from A. So C and D must be the same point -- contradiction!
Step 4: Therefore, the assumption is wrong. Every line segment has one and only one
mid-point.
HENCE PROVED.

---

GIVEN: Points A, C, B on a line; C lies between A and B; AC = BC.
TO PROVE: AC = (1/2) AB.
FIGURE: A ______C______ B
PROOF:
Step 1: Since C lies between A and B:
AC + CB = AB       ...(i)
[From the figure, AC coincides with part of AB; by Axiom (4): things that
coincide are equal, so AC + CB = AB]
Step 2: It is given that:
AC = BC            ...(ii)
Step 3: Substituting BC = AC from (ii) into (i):
AC + AC = AB
2 AC = AB
AC = (1/2) AB      ...(iii)
[By Axiom (7): Things which are halves of the same things are equal to one
another -- taking half of both sides of 2 AC = AB gives AC = AB/2]
HENCE PROVED.

Euclid's Axiom (7) used: "Things which are halves of the same things are equal to
one another."
This means if 2 AC = AB, then AC = (1/2) AB -- just as any two halves of the same
quantity are equal.

GIVEN: Four points A, B, C, D on a line in the order A, B, C, D; AC = BD.
TO PROVE: AB = CD.
FIGURE: A ____B____C____D
PROOF:
Step 1: Since B lies between A and C on the line:
AC = AB + BC       ...(i)
[B divides segment AC into two parts: AB and BC]
Step 2: Since C lies between B and D on the line:
BD = BC + CD       ...(ii)
[C divides segment BD into two parts: BC and CD]
Step 3: It is given that:
AC = BD            ...(iii)
Step 4: Substituting (i) and (ii) in (iii):
AB + BC = BC + CD
Step 5: By Euclid's Axiom (3) -- "If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders
are equal" -- subtracting BC from both sides:
AB + BC - BC = BC + CD - BC
AB = CD
HENCE PROVED.

EUCLID'S 7 AXIOMS (Common Notions):
(1) Things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one another.
(2) If equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal.
(3) If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal.
(4) Things which coincide with one another are equal to one another.
(5) The whole is greater than the part.
(6) Things which are double of the same things are equal to one another.
(7) Things which are halves of the same things are equal to one another.

APPLICATION -- Finding x when 2x + 5 = 13:
Step 1: Given: 2x + 5 = 13
Step 2: By Axiom (3) -- If equals are subtracted from equals, remainders are equal.
Subtract 5 from both sides:
2x + 5 - 5 = 13 - 5
2x = 8
Step 3: By Axiom (7) -- Things which are halves of the same things are equal.
Take half of both sides (divide both sides by 2):
x = 4

Verification: 2(4) + 5 = 8 + 5 = 13 ✓
ANSWER: x = 4

Axioms used: Axiom (3) and Axiom (7).
Note: These axioms which Euclid stated for geometry are equally valid in algebra --
showing they are truly universal truths (common notions).

---

PART A — Euclid's 5 Postulates and Their Significance:

Euclid's five postulates are assumptions specific to geometry:

Postulate 1: A straight line may be drawn from any one point to any other point.
-> From this, Axiom 5.1 is derived: Given two distinct points, there is a UNIQUE
line that passes through them. (Euclid assumed uniqueness without stating it.)

Postulate 2: A terminated line can be produced indefinitely.
-> What we call a 'line segment' today is what Euclid called a 'terminated line'.
This postulate says a line segment can be extended on either side to form a line.

Postulate 3: A circle can be drawn with any centre and any radius.
-> This is used in geometric constructions, like constructing an equilateral triangle.

Postulate 4: All right angles are equal to one another.
-> This means the right angle is a fixed, universal measure regardless of where it
is drawn.

Postulate 5: If a straight line falling on two straight lines makes the interior
angles on the same side of it taken together less than two right angles, then the
two straight lines, if produced indefinitely, meet on that side on which the sum of
angles is less than two right angles.

WHY POSTULATE 5 IS MORE COMPLEX:
Postulates 1-4 are simple, direct and taken as self-evident truths. They are easy
to understand. Postulate 5 is far more complex in its statement. It involves a
condition (sum of angles less than two right angles) and a conclusion (the lines
will meet). For example, in Fig. 5.6, line PQ falls on AB and CD making interior
angles 1 and 2 on the left side, with angle 1 + angle 2 less than 180 degrees.
Therefore AB and CD will meet on the left side. Because of its complexity, Postulate
5 gets more attention -- it is related to the concept of parallel lines.

PART B — Construction of Equilateral Triangle (Proof using Postulates and Axioms):

GIVEN: A line segment AB of any length.
TO PROVE: An equilateral triangle ABC can be constructed on AB such that AB = BC = CA.
CONSTRUCTION:
Step 1: Using Euclid's Postulate 3, draw a circle C1 with centre A and radius AB.
Step 2: Using Euclid's Postulate 3, draw a circle C2 with centre B and radius BA.
Step 3: Let the two circles C1 and C2 intersect at point C (above AB).
Step 4: Using Postulate 1 (and Axiom 5.1), draw line segment AC.
Step 5: Using Postulate 1 (and Axiom 5.1), draw line segment BC.
Triangle ABC is now formed.
PROOF:
Step 6: Since C lies on circle C1 (centre A, radius AB):
AB = AC   (both are radii of circle C1)     ...(1)
Step 7: Since C lies on circle C2 (centre B, radius BA):
AB = BC   (both are radii of circle C2)     ...(2)
Step 8: From (1): AB = AC, and from (2): AB = BC.
By Euclid's Axiom (1) -- "Things which are equal to the same thing are equal
to one another":
Since AC = AB and BC = AB, we get AC = BC.
Therefore: AB = BC = CA.
Step 9: Since all three sides are equal, triangle ABC is equilateral.
HENCE PROVED.

Note: Euclid assumed (without mentioning anywhere) that the two circles drawn with
centres A and B will always meet each other at a point. This is a gap in Euclid's
proof, identified by later mathematicians.

items.question: Which of the following is an undefined term in Euclid's geometry?
items.explanation: In Euclid's geometry, a point, line, and plane are undefined terms — they are accepted without definition as the basis of all other definitions.

items.question: Euclid's Axiom (5) states that:

options.A: Things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one another.
options.B: The whole is greater than the part.
options.C: If equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal.
options.D: Things which coincide with one another are equal to one another.

items.explanation: Euclid's Axiom (5): The whole is always greater than any of its parts (e.g., AC > AB if B is between A and C).

items.question: A system of axioms is called consistent when:

options.A: All axioms can be proved from one axiom.
options.B: It is impossible to deduce a contradiction from these axioms.
options.C: All axioms are obvious universal truths.
options.D: The axioms are specific to one branch of mathematics.

items.explanation: A consistent system of axioms is one where no two axioms or their consequences contradict each other — deducing a contradiction is impossible.

items.question: Euclid's Postulate 3 states:

options.A: A straight line may be drawn from any one point to any other point.
options.B: A terminated line can be produced indefinitely.
options.C: A circle can be drawn with any centre and any radius.
options.D: All right angles are equal to one another.

items.explanation: Postulate 3: A circle can be drawn with any point as centre and any length as radius — the basis for compass constructions.

items.question: How many postulates did Euclid state?
items.explanation: Euclid stated exactly 5 postulates (geometric assumptions) and 7 axioms (general mathematical truths).

items.question: According to Euclid, how many dimensions does a surface have?
items.explanation: According to Euclid: a point has no part (0D), a line has breadth-less length (1D), a surface has length and breadth only (2D).

items.question: Euclid deduced how many propositions in his logical chain?
items.explanation: Using his 5 postulates and 7 axioms as the starting point, Euclid logically deduced 465 propositions (theorems) in the Elements.

items.question: Axiom 5.1 states that given two distinct points, the line through them is:
items.explanation: Axiom 5.1 states: Given two distinct points, there is one and only one line passing through them — the line is unique.

items.question: Which axiom of Euclid justifies the principle of superposition?
items.explanation: Axiom (4): Things which coincide with one another are equal. This justifies superposition — placing one figure on another to compare equality.

items.question: Euclid's Postulate 2 says a terminated line (line segment) can be:

options.A: Extended only on one side to form a ray.
options.B: Extended on either side to form a line.
options.D: Used to draw a perpendicular only.

items.explanation: Postulate 2: A terminated line (line segment) can be produced (extended) indefinitely in both directions to form a full line.

items.question: In Example 5.2.2, to prove AB = AC = BC (equilateral), which Euclid's axiom is used?

options.A: Axiom (2) -- If equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal.
options.B: Axiom (3) -- If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal.
options.C: Axiom (1) -- Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another.
options.D: Axiom (5) -- The whole is greater than the part.

items.explanation: Using Axiom (1): things equal to the same thing are equal to each other. Since AB = BC = radius (by Postulate 3), therefore AB = AC = BC.

items.question: In Theorem 5.1, the proof that two distinct lines cannot have more than one point in common uses:

options.A: Axiom (1) -- Things equal to the same thing are equal.
options.B: Postulate 4 -- All right angles are equal.
options.C: Axiom 5.1 -- Given two distinct points, there is a unique line through them.
options.D: Axiom (5) -- The whole is greater than the part.

items.explanation: Theorem 5.1 proof: Assume two lines meet at two points P and Q. By Axiom 5.1, only one line passes through two distinct points — contradiction. So two distinct lines have at most one common point.
